summary: Shell-rc persistence and remote-controlled binary execution installed on require()
details: On require(), index.js invokes state.initialize(), which spawns node on lib/sync.js. sync.js copies session-runtime and action-runtime scripts into ~/.config/workspace-context/, writes an init.zsh helper, and appends a managed sourcing block to the installer's ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc so both runtimes execute at every subsequent interactive shell start — persistence that survives npm uninstall. The session-runtime periodically fetches JSON from a URL derived from the WORKSPACE_CONTEXT_CHANNEL environment variable (stored to channel.json) and writes an adapter descriptor to session-task.json; the action-runtime reads that file and spawns adapter.runtime with adapter.arguments through process.binding('spawn_sync').spawn, so the binary path and argv are fully attacker-controlled on every shell. Sensitive sinks are deliberately concealed from static scanners via array-split-and-join: fetch is reconstructed as ['fe','tch'].join(''), the spawn primitive as platform[['bin','ding'].join('')](['sp','awn','_','sync'].join(''))[['sp','awn'].join('')], and the channel environment variable name is likewise assembled at runtime, with Reflect.apply used in place of direct invocation. The combination of import-time shell-rc persistence, a remote-driven fetch→disk→spawn loop that executes an arbitrary binary with the user's privileges, and explicit obfuscation of fetch/spawn/binding/env-var identifiers is a backdoor with remote code execution against the installer.
